strengths: The paper addresses an important computer vision and accessibility problem: preserving fingerspelled names and technical terms while incorporating complementary mouth cues into sign language translation.

Specialized manual and lipreading predictors followed by fusion and language decoding form a plausible modular approach. The reported results are substantial: 23.5 BLEU-4 on How2Sign versus the strongest listed baseline's 15.5, and 73.2% letter accuracy on ChicagoFSWildPlus.

The experiments explore modality removal, LLM choice, pseudo-gloss construction, and temporal shifts. Supplementary examples expose intermediate predictions and include translation failures, providing some interpretability.
weaknesses: The central asynchronous-fusion mechanism is not sufficiently specified. Equation 7 produces lip features of length T′ after temporal downsampling, whereas Equation 9 produces manual features of length T; Equation 11 combines them elementwise without explaining length reconciliation or alignment. Its gate weights modalities at corresponding positions rather than explicitly selecting temporal offsets. A subsequent transformer may learn temporal dependencies, but the implementation underlying Table 6's distinct 'learned alignment' condition is undefined.

Sequence routing is internally inconsistent. Equations 3–5 average over an entire clip and produce one class decision, whereas Equation 9 and the supplementary visualizations describe decisions changing over time. Window length, stride, segment construction, and boundary handling are unspecified. The reported 99.2% classification accuracy lacks a documented evaluation set, label-generation procedure, or class distribution.

Essential supervision is unexplained. Equation 14 requires separate targets for signs, fingerspelling, and lip phonemes, but the paper does not explain how these targets and their corresponding segments are obtained from sentence-level video–text data. Converting English translations into phonemes does not establish that those phonemes are visibly mouthed by the signer. Automatically generated pseudo-glosses are compatible with avoiding manual gloss annotation, but their construction, generating LLM, and prompts must be documented.

The experiments are not reproducible from the supplied manuscript. Missing details include explicit dataset splits and overlap controls, training schedules and learning rates, backbone configurations, fusion dimensions, decoding settings, and metric implementations. The LLM interface alternates between contextual embeddings, decoded fusion tokens, and phonemes in different descriptions. Figure 1's caption describes phoneme reconstruction using CMUdict rather than the complete pipeline shown in the figure.

The ablations do not establish the main causal claims. There is no removal of the dedicated fingerspelling branch or routing classifier, no matched comparison against a unified predictor, and no lip-only baseline. Table 6 does not state whether shifted variants are retrained or perturbed only at inference, and the prose specifies offsets inconsistent with its labels. Aggregate BLEU and isolated fingerspelling accuracy also do not directly demonstrate improved proper-name preservation within continuous translation.

The state-of-the-art comparisons lack sufficient protocol accounting: external pretraining, supervision, and evaluation compatibility across baselines are not documented. Attribution also needs correction: the bibliography lists the same 2019 iterative-attention paper with conflicting author lists, and the citation used for ViT-base is titled as an autonomous-driving mapping paper. These issues, combined with unresolved method and supervision details, prevent the large reported gains from supporting a convincing acceptance case.

strengths: The paper addresses an important SLT problem: preserving fingerspelled names and technical terms while exploiting complementary mouth cues. Specialized recognition streams are a plausible approach with potential accessibility benefits.

The reported results are substantial: 23.5 BLEU-4 on How2Sign versus 15.5 for the strongest listed comparator, and 73.2% letter accuracy on ChicagoFSWildPlus versus 71.1%. Table 3 reports sizeable improvements from lipreading and the LLM, providing preliminary support for their usefulness.

The evaluation includes component, LLM, pseudo-glossing, and temporal-shift ablations. The supplementary examples expose intermediate predictions and include failures, making the intended operation easier to understand.
weaknesses: The central asynchronous-fusion mechanism is not adequately specified. Equation 7 temporally downsamples the lip stream to T′, whereas the manual stream retains T; Equation 11 combines them elementwise without explaining how their lengths or timestamps are reconciled. Equations 10–12 describe a same-position gate followed by a standard transformer, but do not specify the claimed learned temporal alignment. Table 6 therefore evaluates a mechanism whose implementation and distinction from the no-shift baseline remain unclear. Its accompanying text also inconsistently identifies five-frame shifts as three frames and ten-frame shifts as five frames.

Essential supervision is unexplained. Training requires sign/fingerspelling/rest class labels, fingerspelling targets, and lip-phoneme targets, but the manuscript does not describe how these are obtained for continuous sentence-level training data. Spoken-English phoneme sequences cannot simply be assumed to match ASL mouthings or grammatical mouth gestures. Likewise, the classifier averages features over an entire input sequence in Equation 3, while Equation 9 and the supplementary plots require temporally varying routing; the windowing, segmentation, and label construction needed to connect these descriptions are missing.

The reported benchmark improvements cannot be assessed confidently from the experimental protocol. The paper does not specify the actual training/validation/test partitions used, how pretraining data are restricted relative to evaluation sets, whether baseline numbers are reproduced or quoted under matching conditions, or precise letter-accuracy and BLEU computation settings. The 99.2% sequence-classification result has no identified evaluation set, class distribution, or per-class breakdown. These omissions leave comparability and generalization unresolved; they are not evidence that leakage occurred.

Reproducibility is substantially limited. Beyond naming Adam and describing training stages, the paper omits learning rates, training durations, batch sizes, temporal sampling, key backbone and fusion configurations, decoding settings, and the exact LLM input interface. LLM-based pseudo-gloss construction lacks a prompt and reproducible procedure, despite Table 5 reporting 23.5 BLEU-4 with this component versus 9.6 without glossing. Automatically generated pseudo-glosses can be compatible with avoiding manual gloss annotation, but this decisive source of supervision needs much clearer documentation.

The experiments do not isolate the main claimed advantages over a monolithic system. There is no matched comparison using the same pretraining data, LLM, and pseudo-gloss supervision without specialized routing, nor an ablation removing the dedicated fingerspelling expert. Aggregate translation scores and isolated fingerspelling accuracy do not establish improved preservation of names and technical terms within continuous translation. The supplementary examples are useful illustrations, but a targeted evaluation is needed to substantiate that central claim.

Several presentation and attribution inconsistencies further obstruct verification. Figure 1 depicts the full multi-stream architecture, but its caption describes a lipreading-only phoneme-to-word pipeline and training alternatives inconsistent with the main staged account. Table 5's caption identifies five random words as optimal although seven scores higher. The references list the same 2019 iterative-attention paper with different author lists, making attribution ambiguous. These corrections alone would not justify rejection; the decisive concerns are the underspecified method, supervision, and evaluation supporting the paper's central claims.

strengths: The paper addresses an important SLT problem: preserving fingerspelled names and technical terms while exploiting complementary mouth cues. Specialized predictors followed by contextual language decoding are a plausible approach with practical value.

The reported results are promising: 23.5 BLEU-4 on How2Sign versus 15.5 for the strongest listed baseline, and 73.2% letter accuracy on ChicagoFSWildPlus versus 71.1%. Improvements are reported across multiple translation metrics.

The experiments examine lipreading, LLM decoding, model size, pseudo-gloss construction, and temporal offsets. In particular, removing lipreading reduces BLEU-4 from 23.5 to 16.6, providing preliminary evidence that the additional visual stream contributes useful information.
The supplementary material exposes intermediate expert outputs and includes unsuccessful translations, helping illustrate both the intended behavior and remaining errors.
weaknesses: The central temporal-alignment contribution is not adequately specified. Equation 7 downsamples lip features to T′, whereas Equations 9–11 combine them elementwise with manual features of length T without defining resampling or correspondence. The gate in Equation 10 weights modalities at corresponding positions; it does not itself learn temporal offsets. A subsequent transformer could model temporal context, but the distinction between the 'No shift' and 'Learned alignment' variants in Table 6 is unclear. These omissions prevent assessment of the main mechanism.

Routing and supervision are underspecified. Equation 3 averages across an entire clip and predicts one sequence class, while later descriptions and supplementary plots require routing that changes over time. Windowing, stride, boundary handling, and the source of sign/fingerspelling/rest labels are absent. Likewise, the paper does not explain how the listed datasets provide the phoneme targets used to train the lipreading expert. English translation phonemes cannot simply be assumed to correspond to the signer's mouth movements.

The experimental protocol is insufficiently documented to substantiate the large gains. Train/validation/test partitions, signer separation, checkpoint selection, decoding settings, the precise letter-accuracy definition, and the ROUGE variant are unspecified. Baseline pretraining resources are not compared against the proposed YouTube-ASL and ChicagoFSWildPlus pretraining. The 99.2% routing accuracy lacks a clearly identified evaluation set, class distribution, and annotation procedure.

The ablations do not isolate the claimed benefit of specialized manual experts. There is no comparison removing the fingerspelling branch or replacing routing with a shared manual predictor under comparable training conditions. A lipreading-only comparison would also clarify how much translation performance depends on manual signing. Table 5 shows a particularly large change from no glossing (9.6 BLEU-4) to LLM glossing (23.5), but the gloss-generation model, prompt, selection procedure, and training settings are missing. Automatically generated pseudo-glosses are compatible with avoiding manual gloss annotation, but their dominant contribution needs clearer analysis.

Reproduction is further hindered by missing backbone configurations, fusion dimensions and depth, learning rates, batch sizes, training durations, and the exact fusion-to-LLM interface. Figure 1's caption describes phoneme-to-word reconstruction rather than the depicted full pipeline; its LLM freezing indication also conflicts with the fine-tuning description. Table 6's textual offset definitions disagree with its labels. Attribution needs correction as well: the bibliography lists the same iterative-attention paper with conflicting author lists. Some presentation errors are minor individually, but the methodological inconsistencies affect the scientific case.

strengths: The paper addresses an important SLT problem: preserving fingerspelled names and technical terms while exploiting complementary mouth movements. Separating these recognition tasks before translation is a sensible architectural direction with practical relevance.

The reported improvements are substantial: 22.1 BLEU-4 on How2Sign versus 15.5 for the strongest listed baseline, 6.8 versus 2.6 on BOBSL, and 73.2% versus 71.1% letter accuracy on ChicagoFSWildPlus. Evaluation covers both sentence translation and fingerspelling, across ASL and BSL datasets.

The experimental analysis extends beyond benchmark comparisons. Component removals, alternative fusion strategies, temporal shifts, LLM variants, and pretraining experiments provide useful evidence. Supplementary Table 9 reports 8.3 BLEU-4 for zero-shot transfer and 13.7 for How2Sign-only training, supporting the value of pretraining.

The supplement supplies pseudo-gloss prompts, phonemization details, optimizer settings, LoRA configuration, and decoding parameters. It also candidly documents proper-name hallucinations and semantic drift, including examples where fluent translations change the intended meaning.
weaknesses: The central routing mechanism is insufficiently specified for continuous signing. Equations 5–6 average features over time and produce one routing vector per sequence, although a sentence can alternate between signing, fingerspelling, and rest. The paper does not explain how segments are obtained, how routing labels are generated, or how segment outputs are reassembled. This is consequential because the claimed dynamic expert selection depends on these operations. The training procedure also needs to explain how independently trained manual experts retain a single shared DINOv2 backbone.

The claimed asynchronicity-aware mechanism is not convincingly established. Equations 10–13 upsample lip features, mix modalities at corresponding timesteps, and then apply a conventional temporal transformer; no explicit learned offset or alignment operator is defined. Such a transformer could accommodate asynchronous evidence, but Table 7 does not explain what changes between 'No shift' and 'Learned alignment,' and the stated shift magnitudes conflict with their descriptions. Supplementary Table 8 shows cross-attention slightly outperforming gating, while the efficiency argument compares the fusion operators without accounting for the retained temporal transformer. These results support useful fusion more clearly than a distinct alignment contribution.

The supervision assumes that phonemized, text-generated pseudo-glosses correspond to observable mouth movements in their temporal order. Neither this assumption nor the pseudo-gloss ordering is validated against signed video. Text-only reordering and proper-noun heuristics cannot establish what was actually mouthed or fingerspelled, which matters for monotonic CTC training. A manually checked sample, pseudo-label quality measurements, and comparisons against unreordered or simpler text targets would strengthen the scientific case.

The experiments do not adequately isolate the proposed three-stream contribution. Table 5 provides lip phoneme accuracy but no lip-only translation baseline using the same fusion/LLM capacity, despite repeatedly identifying lipreading as the dominant source of improvement. Removing the LLM also compares pseudo-gloss output against English, confounding recognition with grammatical reconstruction. Matched lip-only and manual-only translation systems, together with controlled pseudo-label and model-capacity comparisons, are needed to attribute the large gains.

Important evaluation details remain unresolved. The manuscript does not clearly specify split-specific training data for each expert, fusion model, and text-only LLM, including what 'all available' text pairs encompasses; this is a reproducibility concern, not evidence of leakage. It also does not explain how the pseudo-gloss-to-English pipeline produces the character sequence scored on ChicagoFSWildPlus, how a fixed gloss vocabulary preserves unseen fingerspelled names, or how the ASL-trained fingerspelling expert is adapted to BSL. Explicit protocols and task-specific decoding descriptions are necessary to assess the reported comparisons.

Several inconsistencies undermine reproducibility despite the detailed supplement: the main paper describes the LLM variants as fully fine-tuned, whereas the supplement specifies LoRA; expert epoch counts differ between prose and Table 14; and the reported training totals disagree with each other and with the per-stage times. Beyond these correctable reporting issues, the paper lacks targeted fingerspelled-term evaluation within sentence translation and a clearly defined POS accuracy calculation. The supplied qualitative examples demonstrate substantial meaning changes, so aggregate BLEU and POS improvements alone do not establish the claimed high-fidelity translation of critical information.

strengths: The paper addresses an important SLT problem: preserving fingerspelled content and exploiting mouth movements alongside manual signing. The proposed combination of specialized predictors, fusion, and language-model decoding is practically motivated and relevant to computer vision.

Reported improvements are substantial: How2Sign BLEU-4 increases from 15.5 to 22.1, BOBSL from 2.6 to 6.8, and ChicagoFSWildPlus letter accuracy from 71.1% to 73.2%. Evaluation across ASL and BSL provides useful breadth.

The experimental study includes component removals, alternative fusion architectures, LLM sizes, and pretraining configurations. Supplementary Table 9 reports promising How2Sign-only and zero-shot results, while Table 8 establishes that gated fusion substantially outperforms the tested concatenation baseline.

The supplement supplies prompts, optimizer settings, LoRA configuration, and informative intermediate predictions. Its discussion of proper-name hallucination and semantic drift candidly identifies meaningful limitations.
weaknesses: The central asynchronicity claim is insufficiently established. Equations 10–13 upsample lip features, combine modalities at corresponding timesteps, and then apply a standard temporal transformer; the gate itself does not estimate temporal offsets or cross-time correspondences. Table 7 does not clearly specify how 'learned alignment' differs architecturally from 'no shift,' and its description inconsistently identifies shifts as ±5/±10 versus ±3/±5 frames. These experiments do not isolate an alignment-specific contribution. The supplement's O(T) efficiency argument applies to the gate, not the complete fusion module, which retains transformer attention.

The routing mechanism is underspecified for continuous translation. Equation 5 pools over time and predicts one routing vector per sequence, although a sentence can contain signing, fingerspelling, and rest. The paper does not explain how segments are constructed at inference or how segment-level router supervision is obtained from sentence translations. It also describes independent expert training despite a shared trainable DINOv2 backbone, without explaining how the competing training stages preserve both experts. These omissions affect whether the stated pipeline can be reproduced.

The ablations do not establish how much benefit comes from complementary manual information versus lipreading and language modeling. The paper explicitly identifies lipreading as the strongest stream, but provides no lipreading-only translation baseline using the same fusion capacity and LLM. Table 5 compares phoneme accuracy with raw sign-branch BLEU, which cannot answer this question. Matched data, model-capacity, and decoder controls are also needed to attribute the headline gains to the proposed decomposition.

Pseudo-gloss and phoneme supervision need stronger validation. English subtitle rewrites are not verified transcriptions of the actual signs or mouthings, and phonemizing every pseudo-gloss assumes corresponding spoken-word articulations are visually present. Appendix D supplies prompts and examples but no assessment against observed signing or mouthing, and no comparison against simpler text normalization. This matters especially for the claims of linguistically faithful intermediate representations and generalization across ASL and BSL.

Important evaluation details remain unclear. The manuscript does not explicitly document split usage throughout pseudo-label generation and LLM training, despite referring to 'all available' text pairs. It also does not adequately explain how the pseudo-gloss-to-sentence pipeline produces the character sequences evaluated on ChicagoFSWildPlus, including variants without the fingerspelling branch. Letter/phoneme accuracy definitions, BLEU preprocessing, and uncertainty estimates are missing. These gaps limit confidence in benchmark comparability without establishing that leakage or unfair evaluation occurred.

Several reporting inconsistencies weaken reproducibility: Table 6 describes full LLM fine-tuning whereas Appendix D specifies LoRA; expert epoch counts differ between the prose and Table 14; and training costs are variously reported as 108 hours, 240 hours, and stages summing to 168 hours. Attribution also needs correction—for example, GPT-4o is cited to the 2018 GPT paper. These are individually correctable, but the methodological and experimental concerns above require more than editorial revision. Under Algorithms/General, the promising results do not yet provide a sufficiently controlled and reproducible case for acceptance.

strengths: The paper addresses an important computer vision problem: integrating continuous signing, fingerspelling, and mouth movements for sign language translation. Dedicated supervision for these complementary signals is well motivated, and the modular pipeline provides interpretable intermediate predictions.

The reported improvements are substantial: How2Sign BLEU-4 increases from 15.5 to 22.1, BOBSL BLEU-4 from 2.6 to 6.8, and ChicagoFSWildPlus letter accuracy from 71.1% to 73.2%. Evaluation across ASL and BSL broadens the potential significance.

The experimental investigation extends beyond benchmark comparisons. Component removal, alternative fusion mechanisms, language-model sizes, temporal shifts, and pretraining experiments provide useful evidence. In particular, the supplementary results distinguish How2Sign-only training from transfer through YouTube-ASL.

The supplement provides pseudo-gloss prompts, optimization settings, LoRA configuration, and qualitative intermediate outputs. Its explicit discussion of proper-name hallucination and semantic drift is valuable and appropriately acknowledges limitations.
weaknesses: The central routing mechanism is insufficiently specified. Equations (5)–(6) produce one routing vector per sequence through temporal-average pooling, whereas Equation (11) is described as selecting signing, fingerspelling, or rest for individual segments. A sentence can contain all three. The manuscript does not explain segment construction, segment-level training labels, or how predictions are reassembled. It also leaves unclear how independently trained manual experts retain a shared DINOv2 backbone. These are consequential implementation gaps.

The claimed resolution of temporal asynchrony is only partially supported. Equations (10)–(13) perform length resampling, same-time gating, and subsequent self-attention; they do not specify an explicit learned temporal alignment operation. Such a network could learn robustness to offsets, but Table 7 does not clearly explain how 'No shift' differs architecturally or operationally from 'Learned alignment.' Its accompanying text also inconsistently defines the shift magnitudes. Consequently, the experiment does not cleanly establish the proposed alignment mechanism's contribution.

The ablations do not fully isolate the benefit of the three-stream design. Lipreading is identified as the strongest signal, yet no lipreading-only system with the same fusion/LLM decoding capacity is evaluated on translation. Table 5 instead compares phoneme accuracy for lipreading with BLEU for raw sign predictions. Removing the LLM also compares pseudo-gloss output against grammatical English, making that BLEU drop difficult to interpret as evidence of improved semantic recognition. Matched decoder and training-resource controls would strengthen the scientific case.

The linguistic validity of the generated supervision is unverified. Phonemizing an English-derived pseudo-gloss assumes that the signer mouths those words in that order; actual mouthings can be partial or absent, while mouth gestures need not correspond to English speech. The reported phoneme accuracy therefore measures agreement with synthetic targets rather than independently annotated mouth movements. There is no expert audit or target-generation ablation, and adaptation of the ASL fingerspelling expert to BSL's different manual alphabet is not explained.

Evaluation and reproducibility details remain incomplete. The manuscript does not clearly enumerate training/validation/test usage for each visual component and the separately trained text decoder, despite describing training on 'all available' text pairs. This leaves held-out text exclusion unverifiable, without establishing that leakage occurred. The ChicagoFSWildPlus inference path through a pseudo-gloss fusion vocabulary and sentence-generating LLM is also unclear. POS 'accuracy' lacks a precise matching definition, limiting its use as evidence for improved proper-name recognition.

Several reporting inconsistencies need correction: full LLM fine-tuning in the main text versus LoRA in the supplement, conflicting expert-training epoch counts, and computational totals of 108 hours, 240 hours, and table entries summing to 168 hours. Attribution also needs checking, including GPT-4o's citation to a 2018 GPT paper. These are secondary to the methodological concerns, but collectively reduce confidence in reproducibility. Overall, assessed as an Algorithms/General submission, the promising reported gains do not yet outweigh the unresolved mechanism and evaluation issues.
